title: August Visa Bulletin Brings No Relief for Indian Green Card Applicants
excerpt: EB-2 India remains unavailable through the end of fiscal year 2026 while EB-1 and EB-3 categories show zero movement, extending the wait for hundreds of thousands of Indian nationals in the green card queue.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • EB-2 India remains unavailable until October 1, 2026, with no new visa numbers.
  • EB-1 and EB-3 categories show no movement, with backlogs exceeding 12 years.
  • USCIS will use Final Action Dates for August, limiting adjustment of status options.
  • High demand may trigger further retrogression in EB-1 India before fiscal year-end.
  • TPS work permits for thousands temporarily preserved by a federal court ruling.

U.S. Department of State Visa Bulletin

The U.S. Department of State's August 2026 Visa Bulletin delivers another month of stagnation for Indian green card applicants, with the EB-2 category remaining unavailable and both EB-1 and EB-3 seeing no forward movement whatsoever.

The August Numbers

For Indian nationals, the August bulletin is a near-exact replica of July. The EB-1 priority date remains at October 15, 2022, unchanged from last month. EB-2 India continues to show "Unavailable," a status that has persisted since the State Department confirmed in late May that the category had exhausted its fiscal year 2026 allocation. EB-3 India holds at January 1, 2014, representing a backlog of more than 12 years.

Other countries fared slightly better. EB-1 China advanced one month to July 1, 2023. EB-3 for all countries except India and the Philippines moved forward one month to September 1, 2024. But for Indian applicants — who make up the vast majority of the employment-based green card backlog — the bulletin offered nothing new.

"Because worldwide demand is now consuming virtually all available employment-based immigrant visa numbers, India EB-2 and EB-3 applicants are expected to receive very limited visa availability in the coming fiscal year as well."

— WR Immigration, analysis of EB-2 India unavailability

What It Means for the Backlog

The continued freeze underscores a structural problem in the U.S. immigration system. The per-country cap limits nationals of any single country to 7% of total employment-based visas, regardless of demand. India, which generates a disproportionate share of H-1B and employment-based petitions, faces wait times that can stretch decades in some categories.

USCIS confirmed it will use the Final Action Dates chart for employment-based adjustment of status filings in August, meaning applicants must have priority dates earlier than the published cutoffs. For EB-2 India, that option simply does not exist until the new fiscal year.

The State Department has also cautioned that high demand could trigger additional retrogression or make categories unavailable before September 30, particularly in EB-1 India. The filing dates chart — used when USCIS determines there are enough visa numbers to accept new applications — shows EB-2 India at January 15, 2015, but with final action dates unavailable, filed applications cannot be approved until FY 2027.

TPS Work Permits Temporarily Preserved

In a separate but significant development this week, U.S. District Judge Nathaniel Gorton in Boston temporarily blocked the Trump administration from stripping work authorization from tens of thousands of TPS holders and asylum seekers. The ruling, issued on July 22, came after immigrant rights groups and labor unions sued to halt USCIS policies implementing restrictions enacted by Congress in Trump's 2025 tax and spending law.

Impact of Visa Demand on Indian Nationals
›India faces a per-country cap of 7% on employment-based visas.
›High demand is consuming available visa numbers.
›EB-2 and EB-3 allocations expected to remain constrained in FY 2027.
›Employers should explore EB-1 or EB-5 options for eligible employees.

According to Reuters, the order prevents USCIS from cutting short employment authorization for TPS holders from El Salvador, Sudan, and Ukraine, who faced potential loss of work permits as early as July 23. Judge Gorton said he would decide on a longer-term injunction by August 5.

"The ruling ensures that thousands of families will not lose their livelihoods while courts consider whether the administration's policies are legal."

— Skye Perryman, President and CEO, Democracy Forward

Separately, a federal court in New York cleared the way for the termination of TPS for Yemen, with protections set to expire after July 24. The ruling followed the Supreme Court's June 2026 decision permitting TPS terminations for Haiti and Syria.

Looking Ahead

For Indian green card applicants, the October 1 fiscal year reset is the next meaningful milestone. But immigration attorneys warn against optimism: with "Rest of World" demand now absorbing nearly all available visa numbers, India's EB-2 and EB-3 allocations are expected to remain severely constrained in FY 2027.

Employers sponsoring Indian nationals should evaluate whether any employees qualify for EB-1 or other categories with available dates, and consider concurrent filing strategies where eligible. Those with EB-5 set-aside investments, which remain current for India, may find that pathway among the few with near-term availability.
